content.thinking:
I'll design this as a dragonbone soul scythe with League of Legends-style aesthetics — glowing teal/green soul energy against bone with gold and dark metal accents, standing about 2 meters tall. I need it displayed so it touches the floor, either resting on a plinth/stand or laid out, and I'll have to write the whole file carefully in one pass since I can't test the API calls as I go.

For the structure, I'll build a small plinth with a socket base where the scythe's haft rests upright, placing the plinth at floor level with a total height around 2.1 meters. Since the builder requires at least one root joint, I'll add a root joint even for this mostly static weapon, and I'm considering adding a hinge or chain joint for a hanging soul lantern or charm so there's some subtle movement, weighing which role (tentacle vs hinge) best fits a dangling tassel.

For orientation, I'm planning the blade to lie in the X-Y plane extending toward +X with its thickness along Z, so the front view reads clearly as a full crescent silhouette, with the haft running vertically along Y from the plinth up to the blade head. I'm roughing out dimensions now—plinth radius around 0.38 with tiered lathe details, haft spanning y=0.2 to 1.9, and the blade crescent reaching from the top down to about x=0.9, giving a total height near 2.25 meters before I start laying out the blade's 2D outline coordinates.

Working out the crescent shape itself, I'm defining the spine (back edge) and cutting edge as separate bezier curves that sweep from the haft's socket point outward and down to a hooked tip, making sure the two curves don't cross so the closed outline stays valid... Still writing control points...

Computing the curve near t=0.9 gives spine point around (1.288, -0.229), checking the edge curve at the corresponding parameter near the tip to confirm the two curves stay separated and don't cross as they approach the tip.

That makes sense — the concave side faces down-left toward the haft, with the spine as the outer upper-right curve and the edge as the inner lower-left curve, so the edge sitting below the spine at that point is consistent with a valid crescent shape.

Now I'm sorting the outline: spine points first, then edge points from tip to base, dropping the duplicate tip, marking the tip as sharp, and closing the base back to the start. Checking the intersection near the base using the Bezier weights for the edge and spine curves...

At s=0.9 the edge sits around (0.186, -0.041), and the spine at t=0.1 lands around (0.139, 0.218), so they stay well separated — good. I want the blade to sweep a bit more, extending across a span of 1.4 meters to the side, and I'm figuring out how it attaches to the haft: placing the blade origin at the haft axis with a thickness of 0.035 centered there, overlapping slightly at the heel where the haft radius is 0.03.

Working out the overall proportions — total width around 1.4+, with the haft rising to y=2.0 and the blade extending from there up to about y=2.3 total height, which feels right for a heroic scythe (something Senna-esque), even though a real snath is closer to 1.7m.

For the blade material, I'm leaning toward a dragonbone look: ivory-toned with ridged rib segments, and a glowing teal soul-fire core running through a slot in the blade. I'll build this as a second, slightly thinner extrude nested inside the main bone-colored blade extrude to create that inner glow effect.

Now I'm refining the glow approach — instead of a thin glowing strip along the edge, I'll make the inner "soul vein" a narrower crescent that's actually thicker than the blade body so it visibly pokes through like an inlay, plus I'm adding a thin glowing sweep tube along the cutting edge itself using a catmull curve through edge points to create a spectral wire effect.

I'm also planning dragon-vertebrae spikes along the spine: computing spine points and their outward normals manually from the bezier curve (rotating the tangent 90 degrees), then placing small cone spikes at each point facing outward to look like ridged vertebrae.

For the palette I'm leaning into a League-style high-contrast look — ivory bone, dark violet-black metal, gold accents, and a teal-cyan glow for the soul, deciding to use cel-style flat paints for bone and metal since glow effects can't be cel-painted.

Now I'm working out texel density for the painted atlas, settling on a 2048 paint size, and designing the blade's bone-grain texture with radiating ribs and fracture cracks using cell-based line patterns.

For the color gradient, I'm computing an ivory-to-teal tint by measuring each texel's closeness to the blade's cutting edge, approximating distance using sampled edge polyline points for the brute-force lookup.

For the face shading itself, I'm switching to a simpler composed paint: using the wall surfaces normal to detect rim darkness, then layering a cel-shaded mottled bone texture on top using ivory tones for the main faces.

Thinking about the cel-shading on flat faces, though, I realize since normals are perfectly flat the whole face just gets uniformly lit or shadowed depending on which way it faces the key light, so the back of the blade would look flatly dark. Rather than force cel-shading everywhere, I'll reserve it for the rounded 3D parts like the haft and only use manual two-tone painted highlights for the flat blade.

Now I'm planning the parts list and geometry carefully since I can't verify the API as I go, so I need to keep calls simple: starting with a root joint, then a lathed octagonal plinth with a tiered profile rising to a socket collar where the haft base will sit.

Still writing lathe outline...

For the thin gold rim, I'll add a flattened torus geometry instead. For the plinth, I'm thinking dark violet-stone coloring with a mottled texture and cel shading applied on top.

I'm adding eight small glowing rune tiles arranged around the plinth's upper tier, each facing outward at a fixed radius so they ring the structure with a soft gold glow.

Maybe I should increase the segment count to 16 for the plinth to reduce the flat-face ambiguity, placing rune planes at a radius that stays safely inside the vertices regardless of face orientation.

Actually, placing the runes on the horizontal annulus top avoids the phase issue entirely—I can orient each rune radially outward so it reads clearly from a top-down view. Now moving to the haft, I'm sketching the dragonbone shaft shape, keeping it mostly straight with just a subtle curve offset.

Still writing shaft geometry...

For the grip wrap, I'll use a swept tube segment with a diagonal spiral stripe pattern painted on using the sweep parameter, aiming for roughly 4 turns across the grip length to give it a textured leather-and-gold-ring look.

Now I'm thinking about leaving the grip region smooth where it's cut by vertebrae segments, placing those below and above the grip zone. For the top of the haft, I want a socket mount ferrule connecting to the blade — maybe a lathe-formed collar, and I'm considering adding a dragon skull motif clasping the blade's root with glowing teal eyes as a fantastical detail.

I'm working out the skull's orientation: should it face the viewer (+Z) with the blade emerging from its back or side, or should it face toward the blade direction like it's biting down on it? For best readability from the front, I think the skull should face forward, perched atop the haft, with the blade sweeping outward from behind or through its jaws.

I'm settling on the skull positioned at the top of the haft, facing the viewer, with horns curving back asymmetrically as a counterweight to the blade -- a large curved horn on one side balanced against a spiked tail-like curve. I'm sketching out exact coordinates and sizing for the cranium, snout, and blade root so they integrate proportionally with the haft and overall scythe length.

Adding nose detail with small dark nostril bumps, then placing a tapered lower jaw frustum offset below the snout for a slightly open look.

Still working out jaw geometry...

Still placing facial features...

Rather than untangle the exact geometric overlap, I'll just make the horns intentionally asymmetric for a more dynamic silhouette: a shorter, hidden left horn swept back near the cranium, and a longer, dramatic right horn (about 0.5m) curving outward and up for visual balance.

Now I'm defining the right horn's curve using a cubic bezier from its base outward and upward, tapering the radius toward the tip, and shading it with a gradient from bone-white at the base to a darker tan near the tip for a weathered look.

Adding ridge rings along the horn...

Adding three crest spikes along the back of the skull, angled up and back, with smaller ones flanking the center. Now I'm thinking through the bone paint for the cranium using a mottled ivory toon shader, and estimating texel density across the painted surfaces—blade, haft, skull—totaling roughly 3 square meters against a 2048 paint sheet.

For the overall look, I'm leaning toward cel shading on the bone, metal, and gold parts to get that hand-painted LoL contrast, with custom painting reserved for the blade. I'm now settling on the actual color palette: ivory tones with violet-shifted shadows for bone, a deep obsidian violet for dark metal, and warm gold with a darker shadow variant.

I'm also planning a secondary decorative element — a small soul lantern or charm hanging from the haft on a chain, attached via a little gold hook/bracket near the top, with teal as the main glow color and violet as a secondary accent for the wisps.

Now I'm plotting the chain itself: three straight hanging spans with small torus links, ending in a glowing crystal (octahedron or icosahedron) plus a tassel, parented to root with three named segments for the chain joints.

Alternating torus links to form the chain, then adding a glowing crystal lantern with gold caps above and below it.

I'm checking the lantern's position against the blade's reach to confirm there's no overlap, then placing a gold mounting bracket that attaches the chain to the haft around the vertebrae zone, making sure it doesn't conflict with the grip area.

Lantern center settles around y 1.15. Now considering adding small floating soul-wisp spheres near the blade's inner edge—maybe seven tiny teal/violet orbs with teardrop tails as ghostly display effects, keeping them within bounds. Starting to detail the main blade extrude and its bone-paint thickness.

Dropping the tapered thickness idea in favor of a constant 0.026 thickness with a 0.007-0.008 bevel for rounding the rims, using zero smoothing since the outline already has enough points. For the edge, instead of a second thin crescent extrude, I'm sweeping a glowing wire along the edge, and adding a darker, slightly thicker spine band extrude between the spine curve and its offset, giving it a dark-metal look with gold studs.

For the inner offset curve, I'm tapering the width from 0.05 near the base down to 0.012 near the tip, checking that it never crosses the outer edge given the tip's tight curvature — the offset stays under 0.017 near the tip, which is safe. Since both curves share the same tip point, the outline closes cleanly without self-intersection.

Now I'm working out the vein that sits between the spine and edge, with offset boundaries scaling by (1-t) so the vein narrows as the blade tapers — but I realize I need to tie the vein width directly to the local blade width (which shrinks sharply near the tip, from about 0.24 at the base to roughly 0.065 near the tip) rather than using a fixed formula, otherwise it risks poking outside the blade silhouette.

Switching approach: I'll define the spine and edge curves parametrically from base to tip, then build inner features by linearly interpolating between them at a given fraction, which guarantees everything stays inside the blade regardless of taper. The vein becomes a band around the midline with a tapering envelope (using a sine-based width factor) that pinches to a point near both ends, matching up spine and edge endpoints so the shape closes cleanly at base and tip.

For the radial rib lines mimicking dragon-wing bone structure, rather than extruding separate geometry I'll paint them directly onto the blade surface by converting each surface point back into blade-local coordinates. I'll sample a midline curve densely, find the nearest sample for a given point to get its position along the blade, then project that point onto the local spine-to-edge segment to estimate how far across the blade it sits, which gives enough precision to lay down the rib pattern procedurally.

Now I'm defining the paint rules themselves: thin dark ribs spaced periodically with a slight slant tied to the cross-blade position, a bright bevel highlight near the edge, and a shading gradient running from ivory bone tones at the spine to pale icy blue toward the edge, with the walls kept darker than the faces. I'm layering a separate glowing vein extrusion on top for the bioluminescent effect, and confirming the paint function correctly handles mirrored coordinates so both blade faces share the same pattern.

I'm now adding spine spikes — roughly nine bone-colored cones angled forward along the spine with gold bases, placed using a spike helper that builds a capped sweep between a base point and direction, and I'm working out how each spike gets assigned to its nearest skeletal bone for deformation purposes.

The tricky part is that the charm chain joints sit close enough to some static parts — like the haft near y=1.3 — that naive nearest-bone distance could mistakenly attach a static piece to the swinging charm bone instead of the root bone, which would make it jitter incorrectly, so I need to be careful about which bone segment actually wins for each part's position.

To avoid that risk entirely, I'll make every static part explicitly declare `bone: root` rather than relying on nearest-bone computation, wrapping common geometry helper functions so they always pass that option by default, with sweeps, extrudes, lathes, and spikes all taking an explicit bone override.

For the trim details, I'm planning a gold ferrule lathe at the haft top beneath the skull with a dark socket, plus wing-like gold filigree plates extruded at the heel where the blade meets the guard.

I'll skip extra trim around the vein since the teal glow already has its own edge accent, and I'm considering a small circular gold rosette disc as a heel decoration instead.

I'm placing a gold rosette with a teal "soul gem" center at the heel position, checking it sits adjacent to the skull cranium without overlapping. I'm also double-checking the layering thickness of the blade, vein, gold trim, and spine band to make sure they nest properly.

Working through blade origin and skull placement coordinates to confirm the heel span and cranium radius don't collide.

Checking the overall silhouette now: the horn extends the bounding box further right while the blade tip reaches well left, making the piece lopsided but still supported by the centered plinth—total height around 2.45 with width stretching from roughly -0.55 to 1.4.

I'm adding a decorative base where the haft meets the plinth—thinking of four curved bone-claw talons gripping the shaft, sweeping up from the plinth's edge at regular 90-degree intervals to clutch the haft partway up. Writing claw curve geometry...

Below the claws the shaft stays bare and dark, then vertebrae segments begin, spaced along the lower haft before a grip ring, and a longer run of vertebrae up near the top that gradually grow larger toward the skull to suggest a thickening neck.

I'm sizing each vertebra with a slight growth factor and adding small backward-pointing spines on top for a dragon-spine look, skipping side nubs to keep it simple. For the grip section I'm defining its sweep radius and cord-stripe paint, plus gold torus rings capping both ends, and starting a hanging ribbon tassel off the lower grip.

Now I'm designing flowing teal-to-violet ribbons as flat swept shapes with a box cross-section, using catmull-rom paths so they flutter outward from the grip rings with a gradient color transition.

Tracing that top ribbon further down and adding a shorter second strand on a different z-plane, positioned so the charm hook on the +X side avoids any clash—landing on three ribbons total with varied paths. Now moving on to the tassel ends with gold detailing.

For the teal soul wisps, I'm placing seven floating orbs along the inside curve of the blade using low-poly icosahedron shapes, each with a glowing effect and a small trailing spike pointing backward opposite the motion direction.

I'm positioning them slightly below the blade's inner edge curve so they sit within the crescent's silhouette, forming a descending spiral near the blade—floating is fine since nothing needs to hang above. Now I'm thinking through the plinth decoration with a ring of gold inlay lines.

I'm considering painted obsidian scale texturing across the plinth's octagon tiers using a scale-pattern paint function, and also adding a thin glowing teal torus ring near the plinth base for a floor-glow effect.

Positioning that torus ring...

Trying segment counts of 16 for both torus and plinth to minimize the vertex-phase mismatch, since at that resolution the angular differences become small enough that the torus tube stays safely outside the plinth wall regardless of phase alignment.

I'm now sketching the plinth's lathe profile points, defining the step annulus and sloped sections that form the base's tiered shape.

Next I'm adding the teal glowing runes positioned on the annulus band, plus gold trim torus rings marking the step edges and socket base to give the plinth metallic highlights.

Still writing SVG rune code...

For the back plane I'll flip the direction to -Z so the texture reads correctly when viewed from behind, keeping glyph size at 0.05 with 12 total across both sides. I'll make a gold rune texture with three glyph variants for variety, matte rather than glowing since it's an inlay, and skip the dragon scale cards and bone feather ornament idea for now, moving on to painting the skull bone and other parts.

Now I'm defining helper functions for the blade shape: a bezier evaluator and two curves, S for one edge and E for the other, both running from base to tip using matching control points so the blade silhouette is consistent, then checking their midpoint values to confirm the geometry works out.

I'm assembling the full outline array by sampling points along S and E and combining them into the extrude profile, tagging the tip as sharp, and now I need to verify there's no self-intersection in the resulting shape.

Checking t=.95 for the edge curve, I get x≈1.3393, y≈-.368306, comparing against the spine point at the same t to confirm they stay separated near the tip.

Both curves converge at t=1 to the same tip point (1.4,-.45), but their approach tangents differ—the spine comes in steeper than the edge. Looking at the offsets from the tip at t=.95, I'm trying to figure out which side of the tip each curve sits on to determine whether the polygon tapers correctly.

Confirming S sits on the outer side consistently, no self-crossing near the tip. Now I'm figuring out the fraction bands for different features—spine, gold trim, vein—and how they need to taper near the tip where the available width gets very thin, so the bevel needs capping logic to avoid overshooting the shrinking thickness.

For the gold trim range, I'm computing that near t=0.9 the strip width shrinks to around 3mm, which is thin but workable, so I'll cap the trim at t=0.9 rather than letting it run to the exact tip. For the outline, I want to avoid generating a duplicate point at the very tip where outer and inner curves converge, so I'll build the inner point list stopping just short of t=1 instead of relying on deduplication.

I'm sizing the vein geometry relative to the blade — its bevel, glow strength, and a brighter inner core layer with a lighter teal tone — then working out how to place a glowing wire along the cutting edge, offsetting it inward from the blade's thin wall thickness so it sits properly against the edge.

For the edge glow, I'm centering a tapered tube on the edge curve with a soft teal color and moderate glow, built from a smoothed catmull path through the edge points. I decide to skip a translucent aura layer since transparency isn't supported, then move on to adding a gold ferrule collar beneath the skull and considering simple cel-shaded bone textures with mottled cracks for the skull material.

Now I'm defining the ivory and shadow color constants, then setting up the cel-shaded bone paint where both the lit and shadow tones use mottled variations so the skull surface reads as cracked, aged bone under both lighting conditions.

Adding more cel-shaded materials...

Writing blade paint geometry...

Writing blade paint function...

I'm checking that blade coordinates stay relative to the outline origin and confirming wall/rim normals behave correctly on the bevel. For the haft, I'm deciding to make the connecting shaft dark obsidian against ivory vertebrae for contrast, then sketching the shaft's sweep path as a polyline.

Defining rod geometry for haft and grip...

I'm sizing the vertebrae spheres with squashed scale vectors, orienting the gold ring toruses horizontally via a 90° X rotation, and tallying up the part counts: vertebrae clusters, claws, plinth, runes, skull teeth, horns, and blade layers add up to roughly a hundred-plus pieces total.

Adding spikes, glyphs, wisps, charm, and ribbons brings the full part count to around 190, which seems reasonable. I'm also placing small gold studs along the spine band using lerp positioning between front and back points, deciding the part count is still manageable without needing to merge geometries. Now I'm starting to define a coordinate helper function for building out the skull details.

Working out skull anatomy now: positioning the cranium sphere, brow ridge spikes angled outward and down at the eyes, cheek frills pointing back, and a nose horn near the snout tip, each with its own direction vector, length, and radius using bone-colored material. I'm beginning to construct the snout as a frustum box shape.

Checking the socket depth against the cranium ellipsoid surface, I realize the eye sphere would end up mostly hidden inside the geometry at that position, so I need to shift the socket further outward to around x .06, z .06 so it actually protrudes and stays visible.

Verifying the glow eye placement relative to the socket, it protrudes slightly in front so it should still read as visible, and checking against the snout width confirms the eyes sit safely outside the snout bounds. Now working out the lower jaw frustum box placement and dimensions.

Realizing the jaw hinge leaves a gap under the cranium, so I'm adding a quadrate hinge sphere on each side to bridge the connection. Now adding a teal glow rod inside the mouth and verifying it clears the snout's bottom surface at both ends.

Computing teeth base positions along the snout's tapering width and bottom curve, placing downward-pointing spikes at each z-position with length 0.03.

Still working out jaw dimensions for the lower teeth and positioning the fangs at z=.2. I'll skip the tongue since the glow rod handles that visually, and I'm placing small dark nostril spheres protruding slightly at the snout tip.

Now I'm plotting the two horns with bezier curves: the right horn (-X side) sweeps outward and curves up dramatically with a tapering radius, while the left horn mirrors it but stays smaller and tighter against the skull.

I'm adding colored bands along the horn tips for shading, then placing small decorative rings as tori spaced along the right horn's length, oriented using the tangent direction of the horn's curve at each point.

Now I'm adding crest spikes at the back of the skull, then working out the neck and collar geometry connecting the skull to the haft, placing a gold lathe-turned collar around the junction between the cranium base and the haft's top end.

Above that, I'm placing a row of vertebrae segments climbing the neck with increasing radius and small backward spines, plus a gold charm ring with a torus and hook arm near the bottom.

Now I'm defining a hanging charm chain — a root joint with a sequence of chain points dropping straight down, deciding whether to tag them with a "tentacle" or "hinge" role for the joint behavior.

Mapping out the links between those chain points: computing torus positions along the vertical span and assigning each torus to its nearest bone segment, then alternating their rotation so the small gold rings interlock visually.

For the lantern itself, I'm placing an octahedron body stretched vertically, capped top and bottom with small gold cones so the chain feeds into the top cap and the bottom cap mirrors it inverted.

Below the bottom cap I'm adding a short violet spike as a tassel plus a tiny gold ring, then wrapping the body with four thin vertical gold rods positioned diagonally so they sit just outside the octahedron's surface without clipping through it.

All these lantern pieces get tagged as charm3 for the bone/chain binding, with the chain joint sitting slightly above the lantern frame. For the glow, I'm giving the lantern a violet soul-color core with a small white inner sphere instead of the teal glow used elsewhere, and I'm defining the tapering ribbon shape using a radius function that shrinks the ribbon's width along its length for the sweep geometry.

Writing color bands and sweep config...

Checking the curve math more carefully, the underside of the hook sits around y 1.6-2.0 for x in the 0.7-1.1 range, with the tip landing near (1.4, 1.52) — so I need to verify my wisp placements actually fall under the blade's curve rather than floating outside it.

Finalizing the wisp list with alternating teal and violet colors, plus a tail spike direction pointing upper-left along the hook's motion. Checking floor contact and overall bounds to make sure the plinth sits correctly at y=0.

Verifying the curve height at the blade's top using a weighted interpolation, confirming the bounding box spans correctly in x, and checking the haft rod placement relative to the plinth. Working out claw base positions against the plinth's sloped top profile to get accurate heights at given radii.

Now I'm placing claw curves from base to tip using quadratic beziers, tapering radius toward the haft, and adding small knuckle spheres at each claw's base. I'm also fitting a gold ring torus into the plinth top's corner profile and starting to lay out the rune annulus ring at the next height band.

Checking the plinth profile segments for consistency, I'm adding the gold torus for the rune ring and a glow ring lower on the plinth, then considering whether to add corner studs or skull relief details (deciding to skip those) while placing eight bone-spike cones angled outward around the plinth base.

Now I'm reviewing potential issues: making sure sphere geometry scaling works correctly, that lathe options accept the right parameter shapes, and confirming that painted colors on each spike stay within acceptable paint area limits.

I'm also tracking extrude options for required point and thickness parameters, and double-checking the import list so I only reference values actually used in the code, avoiding unused variable errors. I'm settling on the structure for the meta export and the build function signature, along with the spike function's expected input types.

Still writing curve helpers...

Adding gold trim and a central vein strip with an easing envelope so the vein tapers smoothly at both ends rather than ending abruptly.

Glyph sizing feels cramped between gold trim and vein, so I'm shifting them to the outer band between vein and edge instead, placing them around f=.74 with size .05 for better readability, then checking blade width tapering along t to see how the glyph scale needs to adjust at t=.7.

Painted rib lines will run under the vein, hidden where they overlap. For glyph orientation, I'm using the tangent of the blade's midline curve as the "up" direction.

Writing SVG glyph variants...

I'm also adding rune textures for the plinth in teal, with two variants (ring+glyph and diamond), and need to figure out how to pass texture arrays into the card components via the imported svg module.

Still refining geometry details...

Still writing blade shading logic...

The smoothstep math checks out for the rim shading. Now I'm verifying the blade texel density and paint cost, confirming the noise and position arguments are actually used, and working through the extrude wall coordinates and z-order thickness relative to the blade outline origin. I'm also figuring out where the heel rosette center should land in blade coordinates based on the spine curve's position at that point.

Now I'm placing the rosette so it clears the cranium and horn geometry, setting up its gold cylinder base with the rotated axis and the teal gem as two flattened sphere halves offset slightly along z, and adding small gold prongs around the rosette edge.

Checking coordinates, I realize the vein curve at low t values actually overlaps the rosette position near the heel—computing the bezier weights more precisely to see how much the vein path drifts into that region before I finalize placement.

Setting the vein range to [0.22, 0.9], and spacing five glyphs along t from .25 to .61 so they're evenly distributed. Now I'm placing spine studs along the band, alternating z-offsets to give them a slight 3D stagger.

Then I'm designing the spine spikes: each positioned along the curve with an outward-tilted direction blending the normal and tangent, varying length and radius so they taper and peak near the middle, with bases embedded slightly into the band and colored bone.

I check that spike placement near the base doesn't collide with the cranium geometry, and compute tangent vectors numerically by sampling nearby points on the curve. Then I'm assembling the final skeleton structure, setting up the root joint at the origin and verifying each part correctly references its bone, position, and rotation.

Thinking through paint placement: I decide gold bands should sit at the grip ends and collar positions along the haft, and realize paint/shape IDs should be generated fresh inside the build function rather than at module scope to avoid stale references across rebuilds. I'm starting the actual implementation now, importing the builder utilities and path helpers needed for the geometry.

Writing imports and setup...

Defining control points and cubic bezier...

Building the strip outline points...

Writing extrude calls...

Adding a glow effect to the swept wire, and double-checking that the catmull path accepts the point array correctly so the bead wraps the blade edge like a glowing bead near the heel. I'm sketching out the skull helper functions next and confirming the frustum box signature works for the spine spikes.

Now I'm looping through upper and lower teeth on both sides, computing jaw curvature factors to position each tooth's center, height, and half-width along the z-axis, with longer fang teeth at the back and a bone-toned color for the small set of teeth meshes.

Then I'm setting up the horn geometry using a bezier curve for its spine and sweeping a tapered cross-section along it, blending bone and dark-bone bands with a pointed tip and flat base attached to the skull root.

Adding ring details...

Confirming radial/tubular segment counts are fine, then moving to the plinth lathe shape and shaft rod. For wisps, I'm writing a helper that creates a glowing icosahedron orb paired with a tapering spike extending outward, with the spike's base hidden inside the orb.

For orb colors I'm choosing between teal and violet, and considering adding a smaller white core sphere for the larger orb but deciding to skip that complexity and keep it simple with just the outer glow layer. I'm confirming the spike function signature takes a base point, direction, length, and radius, with the direction array correctly inferring as a number array. Now starting on the ribbon helper function, defining its point list, width, and color pair parameters...

Finishing the ribbon function, I note a typing issue: a radius callback returning a two-element array will infer as number[] rather than a tuple, which TypeScript sweep functions expect as a readonly pair, so I need explicit tuple return type annotations or inline literals to avoid type errors—something to watch for when storing radius pairs in variables versus inlining them.

Now I'm laying out the three ribbon curves by coordinates, picking start points just inside the gold grip ring at the top and tracing them downward with teal and violet color pairs, checking that each path begins at a radius slightly within the .04 ring boundary so they read as emerging from under the gold band.

Positioning the gold rings and collars along the haft at specific y-values, defining lathe profiles for the base collar and skull collar, and placing the vertebra segments near the bottom so the claw tips at y=.66 touch the lowest vertebra piece seamlessly.

Adjusting lower vertebra positions to y=0.72, 0.78, 0.83 with scaled sphere heights so they fit just under the ring at 0.87, and spiking the vertebra direction backward. Now setting up a loop placing eight runes around the haft at 45-degree increments using sine/cosine for position.

I'm checking that the plane orientation faces upward and outward with the rune texture alternating between two textures, positioned at 0.2135 to clear the plinth top at 0.21 by about 3.5mm without z-fighting. Then I'm defining the plinth's stone material using a cel-shaded scale pattern with purple tones.

I'm scanning the remaining details — unused helpers, option spreads, triangle counts for the small meshes, and the sweep's glow handling — to make sure nothing breaks when a painted material hits the glow function.

I notice the lantern's inner core sphere would end up hidden inside the opaque octahedron, so I decide to drop it rather than add a sparkle. Then I confirm the charm joint names are unique across the three spans so each part can reference the correct bone.

Now I'm working out which joint each lantern piece attaches to, picking a bone based on height along the chain, and placing a gold hook rod and ring near the top where the first link connects to the root.

Then I'm positioning the lantern's top and bottom cone caps relative to the chain's lowest link, making sure the octahedral body overlaps correctly with both the chain above and the cap below.

I'm also checking that the four gold frame rods don't intersect the octahedron's diagonal edges, which means widening the cone caps so the rods terminate inside their radius instead of floating outside them.

Confirming the rotation order works out so the diagonal alignment holds for both cones. I'll give the lantern a violet glow with a gold frame, and tag all the lantern parts with bone references for rigging.

I'm checking the imports and types used for color mixing (Rgb, mix, paint, mottle) all line up correctly, then moving on to compute the blade geometry sampling points along its spine and edges.

Writing blade coordinate sampling...
